weather.advice:
1. Kapiti Island to D Urville Island approach. Distance approximately 48nm. Head west-southwest across the northern Cook Strait. Watch for large commercial vessels and strong tidal streams. Maintain a lookout for floating debris or logs often found in this area.
2. French Pass (Te Aumiti) Transit. Distance 2nm. This is a critical tidal gate. You must time your arrival for slack water to avoid dangerous whirlpools and currents up to 8 knots. Keep the lighthouse to your port side and stay clear of the Middle Bank shallows.
3. Tasman Bay to Nelson Harbour. Distance 40nm. Once through the pass, head southwest across Tasman Bay. If weather turns, seek shelter in Croisilles Harbour. Approaching Nelson, stay clear of the Boulder Bank and enter via The Cut. Watch for shallow sandbars near the entrance and follow the leading lights into the marina.

Suggested route only. Check official charts, notices to mariners, tides and the latest weather before you sail.

tpl_07a81d3765.label: 1. Check injuries (Assess crew safety first)
Account for all crew members
Check for head injuries and bleeding
Administer immediate first aid
Move crew away from the mast and debris
2. Send distress call (Alert authorities and nearby vessels)
Broadcast a Mayday or Pan-Pan via VHF
Activate EPIRB or PLB
Provide GPS coordinates and status
Monitor radio for response
3. Secure engine (Ensure it is safe to use or turned off)
Shift engine to neutral immediately
Check for lines or rigging over the side
Verify propeller is clear of obstructions
Monitor engine for overheating if running
4. Manage rig (Cut away or secure falling equipment)
4.1 Determine if mast can be salvaged or must be cut
4.1.1 If the mast is threatening to breach the hull below the water, it must be cut carefully.
4.1.2 If it is still on deck, it can likely be saved
4.2 Use bolt cutters or hacksaw on stays if hull is at risk
4.3 Cut sails away to reduce drag
4.4 Lash remaining spars and rigging to the deck
5. Inspect hull (Check for underwater damage)
Check for punctures or cracks below the waterline
Verify that the rudder still functions
Check the bilge for rising water
Confirm bilge pumps are operational
6. Establish propulsion (Get moving safely)
Clear all trailing lines from the water
Start engine once propeller is confirmed clear
Rig a jury rig or emergency sail if possible
Prepare anchor or tow lines
7. Document damage (Record for insurance and rescue)
Take photos of the damage and failed components
Record the exact time and location
Log sea conditions and events leading to failure
Secure broken parts for later inspection

tpl_ebf4ced0d2.label: 1.Trauma & Wound Management - this category addresses the most likely physical injuries encountered in rough sea conditions (cuts, lacerations, and impact injuries).
Severe Bleeding Control: Tourniquets, haemostatic (blood-clotting) gauze, and large pressure dressings.
Wound Closure: Butterfly closures, Steri-Strips, medical-grade skin glue, and a surgical suture/staple kit (if trained).
Dressings & Gauze: Assorted sterile gauze pads, non-adherent dressings, and conformable bandages.
Antiseptics: Iodine or chlorhexidine wipes, alcohol swabs, and antibiotic ointments to prevent marine-born infections. [1, 2, 3, 4]
2.Orthopaedic's & Immobilization (Moving around a pitching vessel increases the risk of severe fractures, sprains, and joint dislocations)
Splints: Moldable foam splints (such as SAM splints) to immobilize limbs.
Support Wraps: Heavy-duty elastic crepe bandages and cohesive compression wraps.
Slings: Triangular bandages for shoulder or arm immobilization. [1, 2, 3]
3.Marine & Environmental Extremes (This category focuses on elements specific to life at sea—wind, sun, friction, and extreme temperatures. )
Burn & Sun Care: Burn gels, hydrocortisone ointments, and high-factor soothing creams for intense sunburns or galley accidents.
Hypothermia Mitigation: Emergency space blankets or thermal rescue bags to retain body heat during shock or exposure.
Eye & Marine Stings: Sterile eye wash solution, eye pads, and vinegar or sting-relief wipes for jellyfish encounters.
4.Systemic & Prescription Medications (A long passage itinerary requires a mini-pharmacy to handle infections, dental issues, and sudden illnesses. )
Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics: Prescription medications targeting skin, respiratory, gastrointestinal, and dental infections.
Advanced Pain Management: Strong prescription analgesics for fractures or severe trauma, alongside standard over-the-counter NSAIDs (Ibuprofen, Paracetamol).
Anaphylaxis & Allergies: Epinephrine auto-injectors (EpiPens), oral antihistamines, and corticosteroid tablets. [1, 2, 3, 4]
5.Gastrointestinal & Motion Sickness (Seasickness and digestive distress can quickly dehydrate and incapacitate a small crew.)
Motion Sickness Remedies: Multiple classes of treatments (e.g., Scopolamine patches, dimenhydrinate, and promethazine).
Stomach Relief: Anti-diarrheal medication (Loperamide), laxatives, and antacids.
Rehydration: Oral electrolyte replacement sachets to handle severe dehydration.
6.Tools, Diagnostics & Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) (The hardware needed to safely evaluate a patient and apply treatments in a marine environment.)
Instruments: Heavy-duty trauma shears (to cut through foul weather gear), sterile tweezers, and safety pins.
Diagnostics: A reliable thermometer, a pulse oximeter, and a blood pressure cuff.
PPE: Nitrile examination gloves, CPR face shields or pocket masks, and hand sanitizer.
Dental Emergency Kit: Temporary filling materials and dental pain drops.

tpl_a0e0de16a7.label: 1.Wound Care & Bleeding
Adhesive bandages: Assorted sizes and shapes (waterproof versions are essential).
Sterile gauze pads: For cleaning and covering larger wounds.
Non-stick dressings: To prevent pulling on healing skin.
Surgical tape: Waterproof tape to secure dressings.
Antiseptic wipes / liquid: For cleaning dirt and saltwater out of cuts.
Butterfly closures / Steri-Strips: To hold deep cuts together.
2.Motion Sickness & Stomach Ailment
Seasickness medication: Antihistamines (like dimenhydrinate or meclizine) or acupressure bands.
Anti-diarrheal medication: To manage sudden stomach bugs.
Antacids: For indigestion and heartburn.
Rehydration salts: Essential for restoring electrolytes after severe seasickness or heat exposure.
3.Fractures, Sprains & Trauma
Elastic bandages (ACE wraps): For wrapping sprains or stabilizing joints on a moving boat.
Triangular bandage: To create a sling for arm or shoulder injuries.
SAM splint: A malleable, lightweight splint to immobilize broken limbs.
Instant cold packs: To reduce swelling from bumps and falls.
4.Marine Bites, Stings & Skin Care
Hydrocortisone cream: For soothing itchy bug bites or mild rashes.
Vinegar: A small bottle specifically for neutralizing certain jellyfish stings.
Aloe vera / Burn gel: For inevitable sunburns or minor galley burns.
High-SPF sunscreen & Lip balm: Preventative care for long days on the water.
5.Medications & Pain Relief
Analgesics: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) and ibuprofen for pain and fever (pack both adult and children's liquid formulas).
Antihistamines: Oral medication for allergic reactions to food, plants, or stings.
Personal prescriptions: A minimum 2-week buffer supply of any daily family medications.
6.Tools & Equipment
Tweezers: For removing splinters, sea urchin spines, or marine debris.
Trauma shears: Blunt-nosed scissors to cut clothing or bandages safely on a rolling sea.
Digital thermometer: To monitor fevers.
CPR face shield: For safe emergency resuscitation.
Nitrile gloves: Multiple pairs to maintain hygiene.
First aid manual: A waterproof basic guide for quick reference.

custom_1793042199068.label: 1. Preparation (before approaching the spot)
Turn on windlass breaker at the DC panel
Remove anchor safety pin and tension
Clear any tangles in the chain locker
Check depth sounder for current tide offset
Confirm hand signals between helm and bow
Ready the secondary anchor if needed
2. The Approach (maneuvering into position)
Scan area for underwater cables and swing room
Turn boat head-to-wind or head-to-current
Bring the vessel to a complete stop
Check chart for bottom type like sand or mud
Identify visual transit marks on shore
3. Deployment (dropping and laying out)
Lower anchor until it hits the seabed
Reverse slowly as chain is paid out
Deploy minimum 5:1 scope for the depth
Let chain settle before snubbing
Ensure chain is running freely through the roller
4. Setting (locking the anchor in place)
Apply slow reverse RPM to dig in the fluke
Check for chain vibration which indicates dragging
Verify the boat holds steady at 2000 RPM
Rig the snubber or bridle to take the load
Ease chain so the windlass is not under tension
5. Final Security (settling for the stay)
Set GPS anchor alarm with appropriate radius
Hoist black anchor ball day shape
Turn on anchor light at dusk
Verify position against shore transits
Log the coordinates and depth
Check for dragging after 15 minutes
TEST extra item
